chapter_theme: Marutham: the wife and her friend answer the straying husband of the field town and refuse his bard (31-39), measuring what his love gave and took through the lily, the bee and the crushed cane; the last verse names a girl of the town by her family's flowers (40).

31.reading: The lord of the town of loud waters, where the bent-horned buffalo wallowing in the field-pond hears the drum beaten against the field workers and runs off with its strength gone, still holds, the speaker says, his rightful bond (கிழமை) with her.
31.nuance: The buffalo that bolts at the field drum invites a reading of the man startled out of his pleasures, but the poem gives only that one match and never states the situation it would point to, so it stays scene; the last word, தோட்டு, does not construe cleanly, and whether the claim of கிழமை is a concession or a bitter irony turns on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo of the field-pond and the field workers' drum are things of the watered fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; the speaker may be the friend

32.reading: The lord of the town of spreading fields of thick-stalked red paddy in ear, where the tall marutham tree with its arrow-straight trunk sheds fragrant pollen on the petals of the blue lily, has fastened a sickness on us too.
32.nuance: எமக்கும், 'on us too', is the barb: the sickness he gives is not hers alone but shared with the women he goes to. The tree that scatters its pollen on whatever lily lies under it reads easily as the man spending his love freely, but only that one correspondence is clear, so it is a near miss for ullurai (condition 3) and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the marutham tree, the field lily and the paddy fields

comparisons.tenor: the straight trunk of the marutham tree, like an arrow shaft
the thick paddy stalks, like bamboo

33.reading: The friend tells the man of the good town of kaanji trees that, like the friendship of the base, he has consumed the young beauty that was his own, and now at the last stands taking in the fresh beauty of the street of bright-breasted women he holds dear as his eyes.
33.nuance: The simile is from the ethics of friendship, not from the fields: a friend who eats while there is something to eat and leaves when it is gone. உடைய, 'your own', makes the wife's youth his property, which makes spending it and turning away a loss to himself as much as to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has turned to the women of the other street and is reproached for it; the kaanji town is of the fields

comparisons.tenor: his enjoying his wife's youth and then turning away from her
the women of the other street, dear to him as his eyes

34.reading: The woman says the lord of the town of fields where red paddy ripens would not, for some days, give his love to any but her; so get up, bard: you have gone into the street of the broad-hipped, bamboo-shouldered women and stand there for your own gain.
34.nuance: The bard is shown not as the husband's go-between to the wife but as one who frequents the other women's street for what it brings him (வாரி). Who speaks is not certain: the other woman could say 'he gives himself to none but me', and the sense of வாரிக்கு is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's visits to the other women's street, in a town of paddy fields

35.reading: The man of the good town of cool fields is like the bent bee that hums over freshly opened flowers in the hot season: he enjoys the young beauty of well-jewelled women and leaves them with nothing but their bodies.
35.nuance: மேனி ஒழிய, 'only the body left', is the point of the simile: the bee takes the honey and the flower stands, emptied. The verse speaks of the women in general (நல்லார்), so the wife counts herself among many.

thinai_evidence.note: the roving husband who leaves women spent, in a town of cool fields

comparisons.tenor: the man who tastes each woman's young beauty and moves on

36.reading: The friend tells the man of the good town of tilled fields where red lotus blooms: if she is hurt, what can anyone do to you, when you are the one who gave and you are the one who took back the fine beauty that came with your giving?
36.nuance: தந்தாயும் நீயே ... கொண்டாயும் நீ: her beauty bloomed from his love, so the one who caused it is the one who has ruined it, and there is no one else to complain to. The question is a reproach that leaves him no answer.

thinai_evidence.note: the red lotus of the tilled fields

37.reading: The woman tells the bard not to come again and again pressing his words: even on the days the lord of the town of paddy fields was joined with us, we of the soft shoulders and bright bangles never had the gracious regard of his eyes that 'our younger sisters' have.
37.nuance: எங்கையர், 'our younger sisters', is the polite family word turned to irony for the women he goes to; நாட்டம், his eyes' regard, is what she says she never had, which makes the bard's assurances of his love pointless.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife turns away the bard who comes for the husband of the paddy-field town

comparisons.tenor: the favour she lacks, which the other women enjoy

38.reading: The woman tells the bard that though he speaks of the goodness of the man of the town of good fields, he need not go on repeating it in practised words; let him stop: the dark hair against which his fine jasmine garland lay tells, by its loosened state, what that man is like.
38.nuance: She sets a sign against the bard's speech: the disordered hair answers his praise without argument. Whose hair it is, the other woman's or her own, the Tamil leaves open, and எல்லு is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard praises the husband of the field town and is refused

39.reading: The lord of the town where, in the dark pond, the big-backed vaalai fish bites at the full-blown blue lily, no longer as on the days he desired us, has eaten up our beauty, and we have become the chewed refuse of sugarcane.
39.nuance: The closing image is the bitterest in the decade: not a flower left standing but the cane-pith spat out after the juice is gone. பெடை may make the biter the female fish, which would point the bite at the other woman rather than the man; the ullurai is tagged on the reading that the fish is the man.

thinai_evidence.note: the pond fish and the blue lily of the watered fields

karu.sense: sugarcane pith, the vehicle of the closing metaphor

the wife, drained and thrown aside

40.reading: This girl, on whom a leaf-skirt of water-lily and a necklace sway, is the daughter of the lord of the town of sweet waters; her garland is of chosen, fragrant, honeyed blue lilies, and the close-petalled lotus is the flower of her brothers.
40.nuance: The flowers are badges: the lily garland is hers, the lotus her brothers'. Naming her father and her brothers' flower tells a suitor she is of a guarded house, which in a love poem reads as a push to seek her openly in marriage; who speaks to whom is not stated.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-lily, lotus and sweet waters of the field town

links.note: Kalittokai 25 likens the woman's eyes, bangles and brow, bright while he is near and failing when he leaves, to the bond of base men who praise to the face and slander behind; Thinaimozhi 33 likens the man himself, who ate her youth and moved on, to the friendship of the base.
links.teaches: Both poems borrow the moral figure of the false friend for a husband's desertion, but the Kalittokai sets it on the wife's changing body while the venba sets it squarely on the man, so the same ethical simile can either describe the damage or name the culprit.

links.note: Kural 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses the friendship of those who are friends while there is profit and leave when there is none; Thinaimozhi 33 calls the husband's conduct exactly such a friendship.
links.teaches: The Kural can shrug at the self-serving friend because a friend can be dropped, but the wife cannot treat a husband with that indifference, since what he consumed was her youth, so the akam poem shows where the maxim's calm stops working.

links.note: In Natrinai 200 the friend, with the bard listening, has the potter cry through the town that women should guard against this bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; in Thinaimozhi 34 the bard is found standing in the other women's street for his own gain.
links.teaches: Read together the two show the bard's double standing in marutham: the man's envoy at the wife's door is, to the town and the wife, a known agent of his affairs elsewhere, and the venba adds that he profits from it.

links.note: Kalittokai 74 opens with a striped bee that has fed on pond flowers and backwater neythal moving on to the field lotus, and says the man joins one woman at forenoon and seeks another by afternoon; Thinaimozhi 35 likens him openly to the bee that sips fresh flowers and leaves the women only their bodies.
links.teaches: What the Kalittokai leaves as an opening scene to be matched with the man's day, the four-line venba states as an explicit simile with its result, the emptied body, showing the hidden image of the longer poem made plain in the later form.

links.note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Thinaimozhi 36 the friend tells the man that he both gave the beauty and took it back.
links.teaches: The Kural's exchange is a loss suffered in separation, but the friend makes the same giving and taking an argument against the husband: since he alone gave and took, there is no one else to blame and nothing anyone can do to him, which turns the woman's lament into an accusation.

links.note: In Naladiyar 390 the wife tells the bard not to lie that the man will be kind, since to him she is the tip of the sugarcane, and to tell it to those who are its middle joints; in Thinaimozhi 37 she tells the bard not to keep pressing, since she never had the gracious regard 'our younger sisters' have.
links.teaches: The same refusal of the bard, by the same speaker, is filed by the Naladiyar under the chaste wife, so the didactic book reads her sharp tongue to the go-between as a mark of karpu, while the akam venba keeps it as wounded pride with the ironic family word for the rivals.

links.note: In Kalittokai 74 the wife answers the bard who praises the man as not loveless by calling the bard, the trusting women, the man and his chariot all deluded; in Thinaimozhi 38 she stops the bard's praise of the man's goodness by pointing to the loosened hair his garland lay on.
links.teaches: Both wives reject the bard's praise of the husband, but the Kalittokai argues the case at length while the venba answers with a single visible sign, so the shorter form shows the refusal resting on evidence rather than rebuttal.

links.note: Naladiyar 390 has the wife call herself the tasteless tip of the sugarcane to the lord of the town; Thinaimozhi 39 has her say she has become the chewed pith of the cane after he ate her beauty.
links.teaches: The marutham wife reaches for sugarcane in both books, but the Naladiyar places her at the less sweet end of a cane still whole, a matter of rank among his women, while the Thinaimozhi has the cane already chewed and spat out, so the same image measures either neglect or use and discard.

links.note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base, like sugarcane, only when crushed; Thinaimozhi 39 has the wife say she has become the crushed cane's refuse.
links.teaches: The Kural looks at crushed cane from the side of the one who extracts the juice, as a way to get use from the mean, while the akam poem speaks from the cane's side, so the same image shows that what is crushed for its sweetness is left as waste.

source_issues: 31-40: no colophon thurai; every speech situation is inferred from the verse.
31 line 4: தோட்டு does not construe cleanly (ear-ring, company, or a corruption); the verse is marked uncertain.
35 line 1: எதிர்மலரேல் தூதும் reads as a corruption of எதிர்மலர்மேல் ஊதும், 'hums over the fresh flower'.
36 line 1: மரைலருஞ் is probably மரைமலரும் (செந்தாமரை மலரும்); line 2 நொந்தான் reads as நொந்தால், 'if she is hurt'.
37 line 2: வயவல லூரன் is probably வயல் ஊரன்.
39 line 1: ஆங்கண கழுமிய may be ஆங்கண் கழுமிய; line 2 பெடைகதூஉம் leaves unclear whether the female fish or the male is the biter.
